claims.text: The baseline catalyst is a nanoscale, equimolar or near-equimolar PtPdRhRuIrOs solid solution with a random elemental distribution.
Pt content can be increased while retaining nanoscale size, support, and synthesis method as controlled variables.
Increasing the relative Pt content shifts the d-band center of PtPdRhRuIrOs.
A Pt-induced d-band-center shift modifies surface ligand and strain effects.
Changes in local electronic structure alter the adsorption energies of catalytic intermediates.
Pt enrichment optimizes adsorption and desorption of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
More favorable intermediate binding reduces the persistence of surface-poisoning species.
Optimized intermediate adsorption can enhance catalytic activity.
Reduced surface poisoning boosts ethanol-oxidation turnover.
Pt enrichment directs selectivity toward desirable partial-oxidation products.
The Pt-enriched alloy will exhibit a lower ethanol-oxidation onset potential than the equimolar baseline.
The Pt-enriched alloy will exhibit higher current density than the equimolar baseline.
The Pt-enriched alloy will shift product distribution toward acetaldehyde and acetic acid rather than full-oxidation products.
The proposed relationship should hold at 60–80 °C under relevant electrolyte and standard potential-cycling conditions.
The proposed relationship should hold only at moderate potentials where metal oxidation and reaction-induced surface alteration are minimal.
Additional dopants or support changes could independently alter the catalyst electronic structure.
X-ray absorption spectroscopy can be used to assess the proposed d-band-center shift.
Failure to observe a measurable d-band shift or consistent activity and selectivity improvements relative to the equimolar control would falsify the hypothesis.
